entries.f9a8d7dde4faba99cc25a392de8bd16d200b1469: <div sID="gen12511" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="111" osisID="Ps.111" sID="Ps.111"/> <div eID="gen12511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12512" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12513" type="x-p"/> This and divers of the psalms that follow it seem to have been penned by David for the service of the church in their solemn feasts, and not upon any particular occasion. This is a psalm of praise. The title of it is "Hallelujah—Praise you the Lord," intimating that we must address ourselves to the use of this psalm with hearts disposed to praise God. It is composed alphabetically, each sentence beginning with a several letter of the Hebrew alphabet, in order exactly, two sentences to each verse, and three a piece to the last two. The psalmist, exhorting to praise God, I. Sets himself for an example, <reference osisRef="Ps.111.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. Furnishes us with matter for praise from the works of God. 1. The greatness of his works and the glory of them. 2. The righteousness of them. 3. The goodness of them. 4. The power of them. 5. The conformity of them to his word of promise. 6. The perpetuity of them. These observations are intermixed, <reference osisRef="Ps.111.2-Ps.111.9">ver. 2-9</reference>. III. He recommends the holy fear of God, and conscientious obedience to his commands, as the most acceptable way of praising God, <reference osisRef="Ps.111.10">ver. 10</reference>.
entries.36c13b63bedda71e6e6ebabebb3d10d4ce18aa01: <div eID="gen12513" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12512" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Excellence of the Divine Works.</title> <div sID="gen12514" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . I will praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with <hi type="italic">my</hi> whole heart, in the assembly of the upright, and <hi type="italic">in</hi> the congregation. <hi type="super">2</hi> The works of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">are</hi> great, sought out of all them that have pleasure therein. <hi type="super">3</hi> His work <hi type="italic">is</hi> honourable and glorious: and his righteousness endureth for ever. <hi type="super">4</hi> He hath made his wonderful works to be remembered: the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> gracious and full of compassion. <hi type="super">5</hi> He hath given meat unto them that fear him: he will ever be mindful of his covenant. <div eID="gen12514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12515" type="x-p"/> The title of the psalm being <hi type="italic">Hallelujah,</hi> the psalmist (as every author ought to have) has an eye to his title, and keeps to his text. <div eID="gen12515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12516" type="x-p"/> I. He resolves to praise God himself, <reference osisRef="Ps.111.1">v. 1</reference>. What duty we call others to we must oblige and excite ourselves to; nay, whatever others do, whether they will praise God or no, we and our houses must determine to do it, we and our hearts; for such is the psalmist's resolution here: <hi type="italic">I will praise the Lord with my whole heart.</hi> My heart, my whole heart, being devoted to his honour, shall be employed in this work; and this <hi type="italic">in the assembly,</hi> or secret, <hi type="italic">of the upright,</hi> in the cabinet-council, <hi type="italic">and in the congregation</hi> of Israelites. Note, We must praise God both in private and in public, in less and greater assemblies, in our own families and in the courts of the Lord's house; but in both it is most comfortable to do it in concert with the upright, who will heartily join in it. Private meetings for devotion should be kept up as well as more public and promiscuous assemblies. <div eID="gen12516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12517" type="x-p"/> II. He recommends to us the <hi type="italic">works of the Lord</hi> as the proper subject of our meditations when we are praising him—the dispensations of his providence towards the world, towards the church, and towards particular persons. 1. God's works are very magnificent, great like himself; there is nothing in them that is mean or trifling: they are the products of infinite wisdom and power, and we must say this upon the first view of them, before we come to enquire more particularly into them, that the <hi type="italic">works of the Lord are great,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.111.2">v. 2</reference>. There is something in them surprising, and that strikes an awe upon us. All the <hi type="italic">works of the Lord</hi> are spoken of as one (<reference osisRef="Ps.111.3">v. 3</reference>); it is <hi type="italic">his work,</hi> such is the beauty and harmony of Providence and so admirably do all its dispensations centre in one design; it was cried to <hi type="italic">the wheels, O wheel!</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.13">Ezek. x. 13</reference>. Take all together, and it is <hi type="italic">honourable and glorious,</hi> and such as becomes him. 2. They are entertaining and exercising to the inquisitive—<hi type="italic">sought out of all those that have pleasure therein.</hi> Note, (1.) All that truly love God have pleasure in his works, and reckon all well that he does; nor do their thoughts dwell upon any subject with more delight than on the works of God, which the more they are looked into the more they give us of a pleasing surprise. (2.) Those that have pleasure in the works of God will not take up with a superficial transient view of them, but will diligently search into them and observe them. In studying both natural and political history we should have this in our eye, to discover the greatness and glory of God's works. (3.) These works of God, that are humbly and diligently sought into, shall be <hi type="italic">sought out;</hi> those that <hi type="italic">seek shall find</hi> (so some read); <hi type="italic">they are found of all those that have pleasure in them,</hi> or found in all their parts, designs, purposes, and several concernments (so Dr. Hammond), for the <hi type="italic">secret of the Lord is with those that fear him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Ps. xxv. 14</reference>. 3. They are all justly and holy; <hi type="italic">His righteousness endures for ever.</hi> Whatever he does, he never did, nor ever will do, any wrong to any of his creatures; and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> his works <hi type="italic">endure for ever</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.14">Eccl. iii. 14</reference>) because the righteousness of them endures. 4. They are admirable and memorable, fit to be registered and kept on record. Much that we do is so trifling that it is not fit to be spoken of or told again; the greatest kindness is to forget it. But notice is to be taken of God's works, and an account to be kept of them (<reference osisRef="Ps.111.4">v. 4</reference>). <hi type="italic">He has made his wonderful works to be remembered;</hi> he has done that which is worthy to be remembered, which cannot but be remembered, and he has instituted ways and means for the keeping of some of them in remembrance, as the deliverance of Israel out of Egypt by the passover. <hi type="italic">He has made himself a memorial by his wonderful works</hi> (so some read it); see <reference osisRef="Isa.63.10">Isa. lxiii. 10</reference>. By that which God did with his <hi type="italic">glorious arm he made himself an everlasting name.</hi> 5. They are very kind. In them the Lord shows that he is <hi type="italic">gracious and full of compassion.</hi> As of the works of creation, so of the works of providence, we must say, They are not only all very great, but all very good. Dr. Hammond takes this to be the name which God has made to himself by his wonderful works, the same with that which he proclaimed to Moses, <hi type="italic">The Lord God is gracious and merciful,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.24.6">Exod. xxiv. 6</reference>. God's pardoning sin is the most wonderful of all his works and which ought to be remembered to his glory. It is a further instance of his grace and compassion that <hi type="italic">he has given meat to those that fear him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.111.5">v. 5</reference>. He gives them their daily bread, food convenient for them; so he does to others by common providence, but to those that fear him he gives it by covenant and in pursuance of the promise, for it follows, <hi type="italic">He will be ever mindful of his covenant;</hi> so that they can taste covenant-love even in common mercies. Some refer this to the manna with which God fed his people Israel in the wilderness, others to the spoil they got from the Egyptians when they came out with great substance, according to the promise, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.14">Gen. xv. 14</reference>. When God <hi type="italic">broke the heads of leviathan</hi> he gave him to be <hi type="italic">meat to his people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.74.14">Ps. lxxiv. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">He has given</hi> prey <hi type="italic">to those that fear him</hi> (so the margin has it), not only fed them, but enriched them, and given their enemies to be a prey to them. 6. They are earnests of what he will do, according to his promise: <hi type="italic">He will ever be mindful of his covenant,</hi> for he has ever been so; and, as he never did, so he never will, let one jot or tittle of it fall to the ground. Though God's people have their infirmities, and are often unmindful of his commands, yet he <hi type="italic">will ever be mindful of his covenant.</hi>
entries.f269ba7c8b6beab265dc2f95a19cd7b66e8ddaf3: <div eID="gen12517" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Happiness of the Righteous.</title> <div sID="gen12518" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> He hath showed his people the power of his works, that he may give them the heritage of the heathen. <hi type="super">7</hi> The works of his hands <hi type="italic">are</hi> verity and judgment; all his commandments <hi type="italic">are</hi> sure. <hi type="super">8</hi> They stand fast for ever and ever, <hi type="italic">and are</hi> done in truth and uprightness. <hi type="super">9</hi> He sent redemption unto his people: he hath commanded his covenant for ever: holy and reverend <hi type="italic">is</hi> his name. <hi type="super">10</hi> The fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do <hi type="italic">his commandments:</hi> his praise endureth for ever. <div eID="gen12518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12519" type="x-p"/> We are here taught to give glory to God, <div eID="gen12519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12520" type="x-p"/> I. For the great things he has done for his people, for his people Israel, of old and of late: <hi type="italic">He has shown his people the power of his works</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.111.6">v. 6</reference>), in what he has wrought for them; many a time he has given proofs of his omnipotence, and shown them what he can do, and that there is nothing too hard for him to do. Two things are specified to show <hi type="italic">the power of his works:</hi>—1. The possession God gave to Israel in the land of Canaan, <hi type="italic">that he might give them,</hi> or in giving them, <hi type="italic">the heritage of the heathen.</hi> This he did in Joshua's time, when the seven nations were subdued, and in David's time, when the neighbouring nations were many of them brought into subjection to Israel and became tributaries to David. Herein God showed his sovereignty, in disposing of kingdoms as he pleases, and his might, in making good his disposals. If God will make the heritage of the heathen to be the heritage of Israel, who can either arraign his counsel or stay his hand? 2. The many deliverances which he wrought for his people when by their iniquities they had sold themselves into the hand of their enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.111.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">He sent redemption unto his people,</hi> not only out of Egypt at first, but often afterwards; and these redemptions were typical of the great redemption which in the fulness of time was to be wrought out by the Lord Jesus, that redemption in Jerusalem which so many waited for. <div eID="gen12520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12521" type="x-p"/> II. For the stability both of his word and of his works, which assure us of the great things he will do for them. 1. What God has done shall never be undone. He will not undo it himself, and men and devils cannot (<reference osisRef="Ps.111.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">The works of his hand are verity and judgment</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.111.8">v. 8</reference>), that is, they <hi type="italic">are done in truth and uprightness;</hi> all he does is consonant to the eternal rules and reasons of equity, all according to the counsel of his wisdom and the purpose of his will, all well done and therefore there is nothing to be altered or amended, but his works are firm and unchangeable. Upon the beginning of his works we may depend for the perfecting of them; work that is done properly will last, will neither go to decay nor sink under the stress that is laid upon it. 2. What God has said shall never be unsaid: <hi type="italic">All his commandments are sure,</hi> all straight and therefore all steady. His purposes, the rule of his actions, shall all have their accomplishment: <hi type="italic">Has he spoken, and will he not make it good?</hi> No doubt he will; whether he commands light or darkness, it is done as he commands. His precepts, the rule of our actions, are unquestionably just and good, and therefore unchangeable and not to be repealed; his promises and threatenings are all sure, and will be made good; nor shall the unbelief of man make either the one or the other of no effect. They are established, and therefore <hi type="italic">they stand fast for ever and ever,</hi> and the scripture cannot be broken. The wise God is never put upon new counsels, nor obliged to take new measures, either in his laws or in his providences. All is said, as all is done, in truth and uprightness, and therefore it is immutable. Men's folly and falsehood make them <hi type="italic">unstable in all their ways,</hi> but infinite wisdom and truth for ever exclude retraction and revocation: <hi type="italic">He has commanded his covenant for ever.</hi> God's covenant is commanded, for he has made it as one that has an incontestable authority to prescribe both what we must do and what we must expect, and an unquestionable ability to perform both what he has promised in the blessings of the covenant and what he has threatened in the curses of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.8">Ps. cv. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen12521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12522" type="x-p"/> III. For the setting up and establishing of religion among men. Because <hi type="italic">holy and reverend is his name, and the fear of</hi> him <hi type="italic">is the beginning of wisdom,</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">his praise endureth for ever,</hi> that is, he is to be everlastingly praised. 1. Because the discoveries of religion tend so much to his honour. Review what he has made known of himself in his word and in his works, and you will see, and say, that God is great and greatly to be feared; for his name is holy, his infinite purity and rectitude appear in all that whereby he has made himself known, and because it is holy therefore it is reverend, and to be thought of and mentioned with a holy awe. Note, What is holy is reverend; the angels have an eye to God's holiness when they cover their faces before him, and nothing is more man's honour than his sanctification. It is in his holy places that God appears most terrible, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.35">Ps. lxviii. 35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.10.3">Lev. x. 3</reference>. 2. Because the dictates of religion tend so much to man's happiness. We have reason to praise God that the matter is so well contrived that our reverence of him and obedience to him are as much our interest as they are our duty. (1.) Our reverence of him is so: <hi type="italic">The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.</hi> It is not only reasonable that we should fear God, because his name is reverend and his nature is holy, but it is advantageous to us. It is wisdom; it will direct us to speak and act as becomes us, in a consistency with ourselves, and for our own benefit. It is the head of wisdom, that is (as we read it), it <hi type="italic">is the beginning of wisdom.</hi> Men can never begin to be wise till they begin to fear God; all true wisdom takes its rise from true religion, and has its foundation in it. Or, as some understand it, it is the chief wisdom, and the most excellent, the first in dignity. It is the principal wisdom, and the principal of wisdom, to worship God and give honour to him as our Father and Master. Those manage well who always act under the government of his holy fear. (2.) Our obedience to him is so: <hi type="italic">A good understanding have all those that do his commandments.</hi> Where the fear of the Lord rules in the heart there will be a constant conscientious care to keep his commandments, not to talk of them, but to do them; and such have a good understanding, that is, [1.] They are well understood; their obedience is graciously accepted as a plain indication of their mind that they do indeed fear God. Compare <reference osisRef="Prov.3.4">Prov. iii. 4</reference>, <hi type="italic">So shalt thou find favour and good understanding.</hi> God and man will look upon those as meaning well, and approve of them, who make conscience of their duty, though they have their mistakes. What is honestly intended shall be well taken. [2.] They understand well. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is a sign that they do understand well. The most obedient are accepted as the most intelligent; those understand themselves and their interest best that make God's law their rule and are in every thing ruled by it. A great understanding those have that know God's commandments and can discourse learnedly of them, but a good understanding have those that do them and walk according to them. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is the way to understand better: <hi type="italic">A good understanding are they to all that do them;</hi> the fear of the Lord and the laws of that give men a good understanding, and are able to make them <hi type="italic">wise unto salvation. If any man will do his will, he shall know</hi> more and more clearly of the doctrine of Christ, <reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">Good success have all those that do them</hi> (so the margin), according to what was promised to Joshua if he would observe to do according to the law. <reference osisRef="Josh.1.8">Josh. i. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">Then thou shalt make thy way prosperous and shalt have good success.</hi> We have reason to praise God, to praise him for ever, for putting man into such a fair way to happiness. Some apply the last words rather to the good man who fears the Lord than to the good God: <hi type="italic">His praise endures for ever.</hi> It is <hi type="italic">not of men</hi> perhaps, <hi type="italic">but</hi> it is <hi type="italic">of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.29">Rom. ii. 29</reference>), and that praise which is of God endures for ever when the praise of men is withered and gone.  <chapter eID="Ps.111"/> <div eID="gen12522" type="x-p"/>

entries.57de3309c9ef82a8352dbf1b90e9cb3b37533f3f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6812"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 111</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.111.1-Ps.111.10">Psa 111:1-10</reference>. The Psalmist celebrates God's gracious dealings with His people, of which a summary statement is given.</title> <div sID="gen10463" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6812"/><hi type="bold">1. Praise ye the Lord--</hi>or, Hallelujah (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.35">Psa 104:35</reference>). This seems to serve as a title to those of the later Psalms, which, like this, set forth God's gracious government and its blessed fruits. This praise claims the<div eID="gen10463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10464" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whole heart--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.86.12">Psa 86:12</reference>), and is rendered publicly.<div eID="gen10464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10465" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upright--</hi>a title of the true Israel (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.11">Psa 32:11</reference>). <div eID="gen10465" type="x-p"/>
entries.e20fb11c7ca9b40f624010ad2100b3fdd283abd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6813"/><div sID="gen10466" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6813"/>2. His works, that is, of providence and grace are<div eID="gen10466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10467" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sought--</hi>or, carefully studied, by all desiring to know them. <div eID="gen10467" type="x-p"/>
entries.68758f3709e3a35e970d028022f32aaf4ceb783c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6814"/><div sID="gen10468" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6814"/><hi type="bold">3-4. honourable and glorious--</hi>literally, "honor and majesty," which illustrate His glorious perfections.<div eID="gen10468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10469" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.7.17">Psa 7:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.1">31:1</reference>), which He has made memorable by wonders of love and mercy, in supplying the wants of His people according to covenant engagements. <div eID="gen10469" type="x-p"/>
entries.4ede5f3680fb6a600c4a1dd9b761b049781aee35: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6815"/><div sID="gen10470" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6815"/>6-8. His power was shown especially in giving them the promised land, and His faithfulness and justice thus displayed are, like His precepts, reliable and of permanent obligation. <div eID="gen10470" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea151dd106850a5dec36da94c1e9462a1572f642: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6816"/><div sID="gen10471" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6816"/>9. The deliverance He provided accorded to His established covenant. Thus He manifested Himself in the sum of His perfections (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.1">Psa 20:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.3">22:3</reference>) worthy of reverence. <div eID="gen10471" type="x-p"/>
entries.4cf8ec08aea2cae04d60e7529afd661b3dfe2446: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6817"/><div sID="gen10472" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6817"/>10. And hence love and fear of such a God is the chief element of true wisdom (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.1.7">Pr 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.10">9:10</reference>). <chapter eID="Ps.111"/>

entries.2983a44c491ba7b1900049954039225694b91d83: <div eID="gen22482" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22483" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22484" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22484" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22483" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22485" type="x-p"/> The psalmist praises the Lord, and extols his works as great, honorable, glorious, and magnificent, <reference osisRef="Psa.111.1-Psa.111.4">Psa 111:1-4</reference>; his providence and kindness to his followers, <reference osisRef="Psa.111.5-Psa.111.8">Psa 111:5-8</reference>; the redemption he has granted to his people, <reference osisRef="Psa.111.9">Psa 111:9</reference>. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, <reference osisRef="Psa.111.10">Psa 111:10</reference>. <div eID="gen22485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22486" type="x-p"/> This is one of the alphabetical or acrostic Psalms: but it is rather different from those we have already seen, as the first eight verses contain each two members; and each member commences with a consecutive letter of the Hebrew alphabet. But the two last verses are composed of three members each, characterized the same way, making twenty-two members or hemistichs in the whole, to each of which a consecutive letter of the alphabet is prefixed. But this division is not proper: it should follow the arrangement in the Hebrew poetry, where every hemistich stands by itself, and each contains a complete sense. The Psalm has no title in the Hebrew, unless the word Hallelujah be considered as such; and the thanksgivings which it contains were probably composed for the benefit of the Jews after their return from captivity. <div eID="gen22486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22487" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen22487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22488" type="x-p"/> I will praise the Lord with my whole heart - If we profess to "sing to the praise and glory of God," the heart, and the whole heart, without division and distraction, must be employed in the work. <div eID="gen22488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22489" type="x-p"/> In the assembly - בסוד besod, in the secret assembly - the private religious meetings for the communion of saints. And in the congregation, עדה edah, the general assembly - the public congregation. There were such meetings as the former ever since God had a Church on the earth; and to convey general information, there must be public assemblies.
entries.a25828db5df3c61c36ff105d3ade6cb9d2b7e1a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen22489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22490" type="x-p"/> The works of the Lord are great - גדלים gedolim, vast in magnitude; as רבים rabbim signifies their multitude and variety. <div eID="gen22490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22491" type="x-p"/> Sought out - Investigated, carefully examined. <div eID="gen22491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22492" type="x-p"/> Of all them that have pleasure therein - By all that delight in them: by every genuine philosopher; every lover of nature; he who traces out the great First Cause by means of his works. And the man that does so will be astonished at the perfections of the Creator, and admire all the operations of his hands.
entries.bbe041bd67fe56e5f395fa422b6cca83bd620052: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen22492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22493" type="x-p"/> His work is honorable, etc. - He has done nothing in nature or grace that does not redound to his own honor and glory; and because all is done in righteousness, it endureth for ever.
entries.35bc7ef3f9e806f9fe79ac176ca6fd14f1ebddf5: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen22493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22494" type="x-p"/> He hath made his wonderful works - He who seeks them out will never forget them; and every thing of God's framing is done in such a way, as to strike the imagination, interest the senses, and charm and edify the intellect. But the psalmist may here intend principally the works of God in behalf of the Jewish people; and particularly in their deliverance from the Babylonish captivity, which this Psalm is supposed to celebrate.
entries.034606db5b74915b12ebb914bd673721be521e8a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen22494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22495" type="x-p"/> He hath given meat - טרף tereph, Prey. This may allude to the quails in the wilderness. The word signifies what is taken in hunting - wild beasts, venison, or fowls of any kind; particularly such as were proper for food. It also signifies spoil taken from enemies. And he may also refer to the wondrous manner in which they were fed and supported during their captivity; and by his support he proved that he was mindful of his covenant. He had promised such blessings; he was faithful to his promises.
entries.b582d143455080c893291e64e30e8d9b1929daf0: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen22495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22496" type="x-p"/> The power of his works - They have seen that these things did not arrive in the common course of nature, it was not by might nor by power, but by the Spirit of the Lord of hosts they were done. And it required a display of the power of God to give them the heritage of the heathen.
entries.b343215f24b7a01728a2cde7ae6409e7f62da9da: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen22496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22497" type="x-p"/> Verity and judgment - His works are verity or truth, because they were wrought for the fulfillment of the promises he made to their fathers. And they were just; for their punishment was in consequence of their infidelities: and the punishment of the Babylonians was only in consequence of their gross iniquities; and in both respects he had proved his work to be according to justice and judgment.
entries.e04499863bd6153b300b7c4398c1258169b2f710: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen22497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22498" type="x-p"/> They stand fast for ever - סמוכים semuchim, they are propped up, buttressed, for ever. They can never fail; for God's power supports his works, and his providence preserves the record of what he has done.
entries.f79cdac867debc2b8ef0a35495c3e1783e7e66be: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen22498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22499" type="x-p"/> He sent redemption - He sent Moses to redeem them out of Egypt; various judges to deliver them out of the hands of their oppressors; Ezra, Nehemiah, and Zerubbabel, to deliver them from Babylon; and the Lord Jesus to redeem a whole lost world from sin, misery, and death. <div eID="gen22499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22500" type="x-p"/> Holy and reverend is his name - The word reverend comes to us from the Latins, reverendus, and is compounded of re, intensive, and vereor, to be feared; and most or right reverend, reverendissimus, signifies to be greatly feared. These terms are now only titles of ecclesiastical respect, especially in the Protestant ministry; but there was a time in which these were no empty titles. Such was the power of the clergy, that, when they walked not in the fear of the Lord, they caused the people to fear, and they themselves were to be feared; but, when the secular power was added to the spiritual, they were then truly reverendi and reverendissimi, to be feared and greatly to be feared. But reverend is not applied to God in this way; nor does the word נורא nora bear this signification; it rather means terrible: Holy and terrible, or holy and tremendous, is his name. This title belongs not to man; nor does any minister, in assuming the title reverend, assume this. Indeed, the word reverend, as now used, gives us a very imperfect conception of the original term. Holy and tremendous is God's name. He is glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders, both in the way of judgment and in the way of mercy.
entries.0d624046aad67466c349b533df94e848b99052f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen22500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22501" type="x-p"/> The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom - The original stands thus: ראשית חכמה יראת יהוה reshith chokmah, yirath Yehovah, The beginning of wisdom is the fear of Jehovah. Wisdom itself begins with this fear; true wisdom has this for its commencement. It is the first ingredient in it, and is an essential part of it. In vain does any man pretend to be wise who does not fear the Lord; and he who fears the Lord departs from evil: he who lives in sin neither fears God, nor is wise. <div eID="gen22501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22502" type="x-p"/> A good understanding have all they that do his commandments - These last words we add as necessary to make up the sense; but there is no need of this expedient, as the words of the original literally read thus: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of Jehovah; good discernment to the doers." That is, They who act according to the dictates of wisdom, the commencement of which is the fear of Jehovah, have a sound understanding, discern their duty and their interest, and live to secure their own peace, their neighbour's good, and God's glory.  <chapter eID="Ps.111"/> <div eID="gen22502" type="x-p"/>

entries.8dd5b099191fb3eae6e3f27fc2029228f02d62d7: <div eID="gen10076" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Alphabetical Song in Praise of God</title> <div sID="gen10077" type="x-p"/> With <reference osisRef="Ps.111.1-Ps.111.10">Psa 111:1-10</reference> begins a trilogy of Hallelujah-Psalms. It may be appended to <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1-Ps.110.7">Psa 110:1-7</reference>, because it places the “for ever” of <reference osisRef="Ps.110.4">Psa 110:4</reference> in broader light in relation to the history of redemption, by stringing praise upon praise of the deeds of Jahve and of His appointments. It stands in the closest relationship to <reference osisRef="Ps.112.1">Psa 112:1</reference>-10. Whilst <reference osisRef="Ps.111.1-Ps.111.10">Psa 111:1-10</reference>, as Hitzig correctly says, celebrates the glory, might, and loving-kindness of Jahve in the circle of the “upright,” <reference osisRef="Ps.112.1-Ps.112.10">Psa 112:1-10</reference> celebrates the glory flowing therefrom and the happiness of the “upright” themselves, of those who fear Jahve. The two Psalms are twin in form as in contents. They are a mixture of materials taken from older Psalms and gnomical utterances; both are sententious, and both alphabetical. Each consists of twenty-two lines with the twenty-two letters of the alphabet at the beginning,<note placement="foot">Böttcher transposes the verses in <reference osisRef="Ps.111.1-Ps.111.10">Psa 111:1-10</reference>, and in <reference osisRef="Ps.112.5">Psa 112:5</reference> corrects יכלכל into וכלכל; in the warmth of his critical zeal he runs against the boundary-posts of the letters marking the order, without observing it.</note> and every line for the most part consists of three words. Both songs are only chains of acrostic lines without any strophic grouping, and therefore cannot be divided out. The analogous accentuation shows how strong is the impression of the close relationship of this twin pair; and both Psalms also close, in <reference osisRef="Ps.111.9">Psa 111:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.111.10">Psa 111:10</reference>, with two verses of three members, being up to this point divided into verses of two members.
entries.1aeb3314648026c4e3591a9456d0d9946fd08acc: <reference osisRef="Ps.111.1-Ps.111.10">Psa 111:1-10</reference> <div eID="gen10077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10078" type="x-p"/> That which the poet purposes doing in <reference osisRef="Ps.111.1">Psa 111:1</reference>, he puts into execution from <reference osisRef="Ps.111.2">Psa 111:2</reference> onwards. ועדה, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.64.7">Psa 64:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.14">Psa 118:14</reference>, is equivalent to ועדתם. According to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.111.10">Psa 111:10</reference></hi>, הפציהם in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.111.2">Psa 111:2</reference> </hi>apparently signifies those who find pleasure in them (the works of God); but חפצי = חפצי (like שׂמחי, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.7">Isa 24:7</reference> = שׂמחי) is less natural than that it should be the construct form of the plural of חפץ, that occurs in three instances, and there was no need for saying that those who make the works of God the object of their research are such as interest themselves in them. We are led to the right meaning by לכל־חפצו in 1Ki 9:11 in comparison with <reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">Isa 44:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.10">Isa 46:10</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Isa 53:10</reference>, where חפץ signifies God’s purpose in accordance with His counsel: constantly searched into, and therefore a worthy object of research (דרשׁ, root דר, to seek to know by rubbing, and in general experimentally, cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">drâ</hi> of knowledge empirically acquired) according to all their aims, i.e., in all phases of that which they have in view. In <reference osisRef="Ps.111.4">Psa 111:4</reference> זכר points to the festival which propagates the remembrance of the deeds of God in the Mosaic age; טרף, <reference osisRef="Ps.111.5">Psa 111:5</reference>, therefore points to the food provided for the Exodus, and to the Passover meal, together with the feast of unleavened bread, this memorial (זכּרון, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.14">Exo 12:14</reference>) of the exemption in faithfulness to the covenant which was experienced in Egypt. This Psalm, says Luther, looks to me as though it had been composed for the festival of Easter. Even from the time of Theodoret and Augustine the thought of the Eucharist has been connected with <reference osisRef="Ps.111.5">Psa 111:5</reference> in the New Testament mind; and it is not without good reason that <reference osisRef="Ps.111.1-Ps.111.10">Psa 111:1-10</reference> has become the Psalm of the church at the celebration of the Lord’s Supper. In connection with הגּיד one is reminded of the Pesach-Haggada. The deed of redemption which it relates has a power that continues in operation; for to the church of Jahve is assigned the victory not only over the peoples of Canaan, but over the whole world. The power of Jahve’s deeds, which He has made known to His people, and which they tell over again among themselves, aims at giving them the inheritance of the peoples. The works of His hands are truth and right, for they are the realization of that which is true and which lasts and verifies itself, and of that which is right, that triumphantly maintains its ground. His ordinances are נאמנים (occasionally pointed נאמנים), established, attested, in themselves and in their results authorizing a firm confidence in their salutariness (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.19.8">Psa 19:8</reference>). סמוּכים, supported, stayed, viz., not outwardly, but in themselves, therefore imperturbable (cf. סמוּך used of the state of mind, <reference osisRef="Ps.112.8">Psa 112:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">Isa 26:3</reference>). עשׂוּים, moulded, arranged, viz., on the part of God, “in truth, and upright;” ישׂר is accusative of the predicate (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.119.37">Psa 119:37</reference>), but without its being clear why it is not pointed וישׁר. If we have understood <reference osisRef="Ps.111.4-Ps.111.6">Psa 111:4-6</reference> correctly, then פּדוּת glances back at the deliverance out of Egypt. Upon this followed the ratification of the covenant on Sinai, which still remains inviolable down to the present time of the poet, and has the holiness and terribleness of the divine Name for a guarantee of its inviolability. The fear of Jahve, this holy and terrible God, is the beginning of wisdom - the motto of the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi> in Job (<reference osisRef="Job.28.28">Job 28:28</reference>) and Proverbs (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.7">Pro 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.9.10">Pro 9:10</reference>), the Books of the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi>. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.111.10">Psa 111:10</reference></hi> goes on in this Proverbs-like strain: the fear of God, which manifests itself in obedience, is to those who practise them (the divine precepts, פקודים) שׂכל טּוב (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.15">Pro 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.4">Pro 3:4</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.22">2Ch 30:22</reference>), a fine sagacity, praiseworthy discernment - such a (dutiful) one partakes of everlasting praise. It is true, in glancing back to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.111.3">Psa 111:3</reference></hi>, תּהלּתו seems to refer to God, but a glance forward to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.112.3">Psa 112:3</reference></hi> shows that the praise of him who fears God is meant. The old observation therefore holds good: <hi type="italic">ubi haec ode desinit, sequens incipit</hi> (Bakius).  <chapter eID="Ps.111"/> <div eID="gen10078" type="x-p"/>

entries.8e9720433c80a8dc7992d71fb8d19f0877d91525:
PSALM 111
This and the subsequent psalms, to the 119th, are supposed to have been sung by the Jews at the celebration of the Passover; and the subject-matter of them was peculiarly adapted to such a purpose. “From the 111th to the 118th psalm, inclusive,” says Jebb, in his recent work on the Psalms, “we find very interesting marks of a ceremonial which, tradition asserts, was observed by the Jews at the eating of the Passover, namely, the singing of the Gospel Hallel — that hymn, in all likelihood, which our blessed Lord sang with his disciples after the Last Supper. Dr Lightfoot informs us that there is considerable discrepancy of opinion among the Jews as to what psalms constituted the Greater Hallel; the various opinions extending or contracting its range from the 113th to the 137th psalm. As usual, these traditions are uncertain and ill defined, and have more respect to the arbitrary dicta of the Rabbins than to the internal evidence of Holy Scripture. Let us now examine this evidence. In the first place, we are to remark, that all the psalms (except the 114th and 118th) which precede the 119th, have Hallelujah (that is, Praise ye the Lord) either prefixed or subjoined, or both, while those which are without this burden are in evident connection; the 119th as evidently beginning a new series. In the absence, then, of any consistent testimony, it seems fair to assume, that this group of psalms formed the Greater Hallel, the sentiment they contain being singularly applicable to the festival, — to the great deliverance from Egypt, which it celebrated, and to the second delivery from Babylon, which so strongly resembled it. According to Dr Lightfoot, the 113th and 114th psalms were sung at one period of the feast, at the second cup; and after the fourth cup, the other psalms, namely, the 115th to the 118th, inclusive; and here the feast ordinarily ended. They thus held the place of grace before or after meat; and this division is very consistent, the latter psalms being more evidently Eucharistical.” — Jebb’s Literal Translation of the Book of Psalms, with Dissertations, volume 2, pages 269-271.
The title to this psalm supplies the place of an argument; and, that others may be induced to engage in the praises of God, the Psalmist points out the manner of doing so by his own example. Then he gives a short account of the manifold benefits which, in olden times, he conferred upon the faithful, and is daily conferring upon them. The psalm is composed in alphabetical order, each verse containing two letters. The first verse begins with a, א aleph, while the letter b, ב beth, is placed at the commencement of the next half of the verse. The last two verses only are not divided into hemistiches; but each of these has three letters. If, however, any one will closely examine the contents, he will find that this has occurred through mistake or inadvertence; for if we make these two verses into three,
“These two verses,” says Dr Geddes, “might just as well have made three, and then the whole of both psalms would be regular.” According to Jerome, this is the first psalm that is exactly alphabetical, the rest of this description, which precede it, being only nearly so.
the construction of the sentences corresponds very well one with another; and consequently, the transcribers have erred in not attending to the prophet’s distinction.
Psalm 111:1-4
1. Praise ye Jehovah.
The Hebrew for Praise ye Jehovah is Hallelujah. This is probably the title, and no part of the psalm itself. The alphabetical construction of the poem seems to confirm this opinion. It is acrostic, and begins with aleph, and each succeeding hemistich commences with the other letters of the alphabet in order; but were Hallelujah, which begins with the fifth letter of the alphabet, answering to our H, the first word of the psalm, that would destroy its perfectly alphabetical character.
(א, aleph,) I will praise Jehovah with my whole heart, (ב, beth) In the congregation and assembly of the just. 2. (ג, gimel,) The works of Jehovah are great, (ד, daleth,) Sought out of all who have a desire to them. 3. (ה, he,) His work is beautiful and magnificent: (ו, vau,) And his justice endureth for ever. 4. (ז, zain,) He hath caused his marvellous works to be remembered: (ח, cheth,) Jehovah is compassionate and merciful.
 
1 I will praise Jehovah The best and most efficient method of inculcating the performance of any duty is to be exemplary; and, accordingly, we find that the prophet, in the present instance, sets himself for an example, to lead others to engage in the celebration of God’s praises. His resolution to praise God consists of two parts; that he would celebrate God’s praises unfeignedly, with all his heart, and that he would do it publicly, in the assembly of the faithful. He very properly begins with heart-praise, because it is much better to praise in secret, and when no one is conscious of it, than to lift up our voice, and shout forth his praises with feigned lips. At the same time, the person who, in secret, pours out his heart in grateful emotions towards God, will also set forth his praises in swelling strains, otherwise God would be deprived of one half of the honor which is due to him. The prophet then determines to praise God with the whole heart, that is, with an upright and honest heart; not that he engages to come up to the full measure of his duty, but he declares that he would not be like the hypocrites, who, coldly and with a double heart, or rather guilefully and perfidiously, employ their lips only in the praises of God. This is a point worthy of notice, lest any should be discouraged, in consequence of not being able to cherish the hope of attaining to that perfection of heart which is so desirable; for however defective our praises may be, they may nevertheless be acceptable to God, provided only we strive unfeignedly to render unto him this act of devotion. We come now to the other part of his resolution, in which he says he would proclaim the praises of God before men; for although the Hebrew term סוד, sod, denotes a private assembly,
“Aben Ezra and others think that עדה is put in opposition to סוד, which denotes a more secret assembly; and so the verse, they say, means, in substance, as follows: ‘I will praise the Lord with all my heart, both privately and publicly.’ This, however, I think can scarcely be the sense: it is much more likely that סוד is here employed to express a congregation of Israelites; because the rest of the world was excluded from such assembly, and so far it partook of the character of private or secret. This is the view taken by Luther, whose paraphrase of this verse is as follows: ‘I thank the Lord here in this public assembly, where we (Israelites) meet one another as in private counsel, and where no heathen nor strangers can be present.’” — Phillips.
yet I think that, in this passage, he employs two words of synonymous import. At the same time, should any one be inclined to take a more refined view of the passage, he may do so if he please. He says, in the congregation of the just, because the principal object for which holy assemblies are convened, is to afford the worshippers of God an opportunity of presenting to him sacrifices of praise, agreeably to what is stated in Psalm 65:1,
“Praise waits for thee, O Jehovah! in Zion.”

entries.1170ac1393fb8a8a84711fe661e5205c7aa173f7:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="111" type="Psalm">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:500" />
                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>The excellency of this Psalm appears, as from other things, so from the Psalmists care to digest the several parcels of it in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to an exact order according to the order of the letters of the Hebrew Alphabet, that it might be better fixed in the memories of those who read it. It is a short yet full com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />memoration of Gods works.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>
                        </ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> PRaise ye the LORD, I will praise the LORD with my whole heart, in the assembly of the upright <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Of the sincere Worshippers of God, of the <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> of God, as this very word is explained, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 23. 10. where they who are called <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> in one clause are called <ns0:hi>righteous</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />right</ns0:hi> in the next. And this title he gives to the Assembly or Congregation of <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> partly because many of them were such, and he was obliged in charity to judge all of them to be so, of whom he had no evidence to the contrary; part<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly because upright persons do most exercise and delight themselves in this duty of praising God, and hypocrites, though sometimes they give themselves to prayer, yet are very apt to neglect the duty of thanksgiving; partly because this duty of <ns0:hi>praise is</ns0:hi> most <ns0:hi>comely for the upright, Psal.</ns0:hi> 33. 1. and partly because <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> heart was most united to the sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cere <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> and his desire was, as far as he could, to as<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sociate himself with such in the worship and service of God.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> the congrega<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 The works of the LORD <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Either, 1. the works of Creation: or rather, 2. the works of his Providence in the World, and especially in and for his Church and people; of which he speaks in the rest of the Psalm.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> great <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">For the infinite power and wisdom and goodness manifested in them.</ns0:note>, sought out <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Highly valued and regard<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, as this very word and phrase is used <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 11. 12. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 62. 12. or frequently called to mind, and diligently me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ditated upon, when others either never regard them, or instantly forget them: or, <ns0:hi>found out,</ns0:hi> as this word is taken <ns0:hi>Isai.</ns0:hi> 65. 1. the antecedent being put for the consequent, which is frequent in Scripture, as <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12. 2. where <ns0:hi>proving</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>trying</ns0:hi> (for so the Greek word there signifies) is put for <ns0:hi>approving,</ns0:hi> which follows after it. And, <ns0:hi>found out, i. e.</ns0:hi> truly and throughly understood, both as to the nature of them, and Gods counsels and ends in them; whereas the works of God are oft-times not apprehended or minded, or are mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />staken and misconstrued, by ungodly men.</ns0:note> of all them that have pleasure therein <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Of all them who take delight in observing and considering the works of God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 His work <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either all his works, of which see the Note <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2. or that eminent branch of those works, his providence to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards his people, as it is expressed afterwards.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. <ns0:hi>honour <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> glory.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> honourable and glori<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Becom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the Divine Majesty, and bringing glory to him from all that observe and consider it.</ns0:note>: and his righteousness <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">His justice or faithfulness in performing his word.</ns0:note> endureth for ever <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Hath always been and will still be evident to his people in all generations and in all condi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions, even when he afflicts them, and seems to deal most severely, and to break his promise with them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 He hath made his wonderful works to be re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />membred <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Either, 1. by those memorials which he hath left of them in his Word: or rather, 2. by their own wonderful nature, and the lasting effects and benefits flowing from them, which are such as cannot easily be forgotten.</ns0:note>: the LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> gracious and full of compassion <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">To<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards his people, as appears from his works and carriage towards us, in sparing and pardoning and restoring and pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serving us when we have deserved to be utterly destroyed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 He hath given <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> prey.</ns0:note> meat <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Which includes all necessary provisions for their being and well-being. The word signifies <ns0:hi>spoil,</ns0:hi> and so may relate to the spoil of the <ns0:hi>Egyptians,</ns0:hi> granted by God to the <ns0:hi>Israe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lites;</ns0:hi> but it is sometimes used for <ns0:hi>food,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 31. 15. <ns0:hi>Mal,</ns0:hi> 3. 10.</ns0:note> unto them that fear him <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> the onely people in the world which feared and worshipped the true God according to his will; and especially to those among them that truly feared God, and, for their sakes, to the body of that Nation, as well in the Wilderness, as in their following straits and mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />series.</ns0:note>: he will ever be <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>he hath ever been;</ns0:hi> for both in the first branch of this verse, and in the foregoing and following verses he is speaking of the former works of God. So the Future tense is put for the past, as it is frequently, and as on the contrary the past tense is oft put for the Future.</ns0:note> mindful of his co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venant <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Which he made with <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> and with his seed for ever; whereby he obliged himself to be their God, and to provide all ne<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessaries for them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 He hath shewed <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Not onely by words, but by his actions.</ns0:note> his people the power of his works <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">His mighty power in his works, and especially in that which here follows.</ns0:note>, that he may give them the heritage of the heathen <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The land of <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> which had been possessed and inhe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rited by the heathens.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 The works of his hands <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">All that he doth either on the behalf of his people, or against his or their enemies; of both which sorts of works he spoke in the foregoing verse.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> verity and judgment <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Are exactly agreeable to his word or promises, and to the rules of justice.</ns0:note>; <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 19. 7.</ns0:note> all his commandments <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Either, 1. his Laws given to the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> especially the Moral Law considered with its sanction, the promises made to the obser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers of it, and the threatnings denounced against transgres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sors. Or, 2. his works, as it is in the first clause, called his <ns0:hi>Commands,</ns0:hi> because they are done by virtue of his decree, and by his power and authority; as in like manner God is said to <ns0:hi>command</ns0:hi> those blessings which he purposeth to give, and doth effectually procure, as <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 28. 8. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 42. 9. & 68. 28. & 133. 3. and to <ns0:hi>command</ns0:hi> those creatures which he moveth and acteth as he pleaseth, as 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 17. 4. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 8. 27.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> sure <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Or <ns0:hi>faithful</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>certain,</ns0:hi> constant and unchangeable, as his Laws are, being grounded upon the immurable rules of justice or equity; infallible and irresistible, as his coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sels and ways are.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 40. 8. Mat. 5. 18.</ns0:note> They <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. are <ns0:hi>esta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />blished.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> stand fast <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>They are established</ns0:hi> upon the sure foundations of truth and uprightness, as it follows.</ns0:note> for ever and ever, <ns0:hi>and are</ns0:hi> done <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Constituted or or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dered.</ns0:note> in truth and uprightness<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 He sent redemption <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">That deliverance out of <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> which was a type and pledge of that greater and higher redemption by Christ.</ns0:note> unto his people, he hath commanded <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Appointed or established firmly by his power and authority. And so this word is oft used, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 33. 9. & 42. 9. & 105. 31. 34. See also before on <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7. the ground of which signification may be taken from hence, that the command of a sufficient authority concerning any thing, doth commonly establish and effect it.</ns0:note> his covenant for ever <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Through all successive generations of his people to the end of the world; for the Covenant is the same for substance in all, and differeth onely in circumstances.</ns0:note>: ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly and reverend <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Terrible to his enemies, and venera<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble in his peoples eyes, and holy in all his dealings with all men.</ns0:note>
